pillar_reactions.evidence: Presented from 00:32:36, opened by calling back his own disclosure — "Remember, you mentioned that you have stiffness in your back, like, from hunching over the phone" — then the standard content: strength, conditioning and mobility as a unit, three to four sessions of 30 to 40 minutes, short daily mobility protocols, less-is-more recovery framing, and the six-month self-sufficiency model. Asked directly he confirmed without elaboration: "Does that make sense? Yep. This approach would actually work for you? Yeah, it would. Of course, yeah... straightforward." One clarifying question followed, about the delivery model rather than the method: "you said he works with each client one-on-one, so I guess I'll be dragged with him directly?" Accepted rather than enthusiastic — he is already running kettlebell circuits at 20 kg and needed no persuading that the modality works, so the pillar largely confirmed a decision he had made on YouTube.

Presented at 00:38:00, prefaced by the rep conceding it was already solved — "what you said sounds that it's pretty dialed in. You eat clean, you intermittent fast, and that's very good" — and then reframed around the one novel claim: "the missing piece may be that you're not eating enough, actually... for the two years that you've been restricting yourself, your gut gets smaller." The prospect did not contest it and did not engage with it either; his only response in the section was "Yeah, I agree" to the impossible-to-overeat-real-food line. This pillar had the least to add of the three by some distance — he runs 14 to 16 hour fasts, two meals a day, 70-80 g of protein at breakfast, has done 60-hour water fasts, and demonstrated he can maintain through two weeks of pasta and pizza in Italy without gaining. The under-eating observation was the only genuinely new input and it was asserted rather than explored.

Presented at 00:40:15 as the app, weekly check-ins, video form review and Trevor's cell number with travel adjustments. He volunteered that this is the entire reason he called, unprompted and twice: "This is the reason I reached out, right? Because listen, he puts enough content out there, right? Like, you can probably piece it together... But it's like, it's the structure, it's the accountability" and "there's enough information out there in the web that you can probably, if you're disciplined enough, do it yourself. But I think... that was the reason I reached out." He then supplied his own worked example of why content alone fails him — the mobility videos he has saved and does not do, and the clean technique he cannot fix from YouTube. Enthusiastic on the definition: he tied the pillar directly to his own goal and did the arguing himself.

anchors.raw: he puts enough content out there, right? Like, you can probably piece it together... there's enough information out there in the web that you can probably, you know, if you're disciplined enough, etc., you can probably do it yourself.
anchors.note: The strongest structural anchor on the call and the most interesting one in the batch, because the prospect raised it and then dismantled it himself in the same breath, landing on structure and accountability as the thing worth paying for. The rep reinforced it with a consultant analogy aimed squarely at a business owner — "in business, you can also find things on YouTube, but it's about the speed and dialing that in... you just shortcut the whole process. So it doesn't take you another two years, it's to take you only six months." That is the correct answer to this anchor and it is the clearest example in the batch of the free-content objection being neutralised rather than avoided.

anchors.raw: I got like bunch of other kettlebells guys on there, but Trevor is probably the best one out of all of them that I have. On YouTube, I'll be very honest.
anchors.note: He has actively compared the competitive set and rated Trevor top. Combined with a month of self-directed practice off the back of those videos, this is a prospect who has already done his own diligence and arrived pre-sold on the practitioner. Note he did not know Trevor's name at the start of the call, so the preference is about the content, not the brand.

anchors.raw: my son plays cricket, he's actually going on a summer tour this summer in about two weeks to London, which is a very big expense, you can imagine, right? It's like a two-week tour, eight games.
anchors.note: A concrete competing claim on the same near-term cash, landing within two weeks, plus heavy travel across July and September. This is the substance of the stated objection — not whether $6,000 is worth it, but whether it can leave the account in the next 30 days. It is also precisely why the interest-free $3,000 plus $3,000 split was the right instrument and why the rep was correct to recommend it.

anchors.raw: you can imagine my wife just, you know, gave birth. She's well out of shape. She needs to get in shape as well, too. And then here I'm telling her, let me, I'm going to go spend money and get in shape. She's like, what about me?
anchors.note: The real spouse objection, stated plainly by the prospect and stronger than the money. It is not scepticism about the programme, it is an equity question inside the household two weeks after a birth. The rep's response amplified it — "She might be opposed to that, actually" — rather than resolving it, and no partner or household option was raised. This is the anchor most likely to decide the Monday follow-up.

anchors.raw: I'm not too concerned about the amount, I'll be very honest. It's a bit more than I had anticipated, right? But $1,000 a month is a reasonable number. It's not too crazy.
anchors.note: The lump sum exceeded his expectation but the monthly framing brought it inside his comfort range immediately — a clean demonstration that for this prospect the barrier is denomination rather than magnitude. It has to be read with a caveat that matters: the figure he judged reasonable, $1,000, is $200 below the $1,200 the rep actually quoted, and he was not corrected. The supportive reading of this anchor is therefore built on a number that was never offered.

anchors.raw: in this two years, right? Like, we've done multiple vacations. One of them was in Italy. All we ate was pasta and pizza for like 14 days, right? And I didn't gain a pound.
anchors.note: Two years of self-directed results — 100 kg to 80 kg, held for a year, plus demonstrated ability to maintain through disruption. He is buying an addition to a working system, not a fix for a broken one, which caps how much of the value case can rest on outcomes he has already achieved alone. It also explains why the nutrition pillar could not do any work here.

unmet_demand.want: Assurance that loaded overhead kettlebell work is appropriate for a right shoulder that was injected with steroid about a month earlier, after physiotherapy failed.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep registered the risk and resolved it entirely inside the product — "the weights that you said, they seem pretty high already. So, definitely, Trevor will check your form." A form check is not an answer to whether the shoulder is cleared for the work. The prospect had already flagged the fragility himself ("that's one thing that could potentially come back") and reported his own doctor saying failure of the injection would mean a bigger problem to fix properly. Nobody proposed involving the treating clinician, and no screening step exists in the offer to catch this.

unmet_demand.want: Something that answers his wife's reasonable objection — she has just given birth, is out of shape herself, and would be watching household money go to his fitness rather than hers.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He named this himself as the likely obstacle and the rep agreed with it rather than addressing it. No partner, couples or household option was mentioned, no way of including her was floated, and nothing was offered that he could take back to that conversation. The corpus shows women are served elsewhere, so this is very likely something that could have been positioned; on this call nobody said anything at all.

unmet_demand.want: A start that works around being away for most of July and most of September, and around newborn-disrupted sleep.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Travel was answered generically — text Trevor and he will adjust the programme — and the busy-season reframe was used to argue that no time is a better time, which is correct as a sales move but does not answer the operational question. No start date was proposed, no deferred-start option was discussed, and the sleep disruption he volunteered at 00:47:55 was acknowledged ("you have two small kids. We have to work around that") without any mechanism attached. Almost certainly accommodatable; nothing concrete was offered.

unmet_demand.want: Clarity on the actual cost of paying monthly.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The monthly option was stated once, at $1,200, inside the most garbled passage of the call, and the prospect twice restated it back as $1,000 without correction. He left to consult his wife on a number that was never quoted to him. Recorded here as demand rather than merely an error because his stated decision criterion is monthly affordability, so the figure is the deciding input.
